report.summary: Incident S08 is inconclusive: payment-service error rate stepped from about 0.2% to 21% at 11:00 UTC and stayed around 20-23% through 11:30, while checkout-service errors rose from about 0.3% to 9.5% in the same bucket. The only change in the two hours before onset is the payment-service v3.2.0 deploy at 10:57 UTC, which is the leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.55) but is unverified. No payment-service log lines could be retrieved because every query timed out, so the error signature, status codes and endpoint concentration are unknown. The schema migration status for v3.2.0 is unrecorded, and payment-provider has no telemetry, so an external provider failure remains a live alternative. Health checks are shallow and do not exercise payment writes, so their green results do not discriminate between candidates. The root cause is therefore not established.

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: The v3.2.0 deploy at 10:57:00Z changed payments table writes (idempotency_key) and upgraded the ORM 5.x to 6.x; if the separately-run schema migration was missing or incomplete, payment writes would fail with 500s from 11:00, and checkout's 500s from payment-service calls follow as downstream propagation. Shallow health checks do not exercise writes, so they stay green.

Schema migration status is unknown and may be incomplete
Checkout 500s originate from payment-service rather than another path

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: The separately-run v3.2.0 schema migration was applied partially or incorrectly, so the new idempotency_key write path fails while the code itself is fine. This is a variant of H1 differing only in whether the fault lies in the migration step.
assumptions: The migration is absent from change history

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: An external provider-side failure or integration rejection starting near 11:00 could surface as payment-service 500s, with checkout propagating them. The sharp onset with flat local latency and CPU fits a discrete external failure.

inferred_conclusions.statement: The v3.2.0 deploy is the leading candidate for the payment-service failure (H1), but it is unverified: the write-path mechanism has not been observed in logs, and timing alone cannot establish causation.

brief.title: payment-service errors
brief.alert: ALERT [P1] payment-service error rate 22% since ~11:00 UTC; payments failing.

plan.incident_understanding: payment-service error rate rose to about 22% starting around 11:00 UTC, with checkout-service also alerting, so payment failures are propagating into checkout. Telemetry covers 10:00 to 11:30 UTC. The cause is unknown; candidates include a recent deployment or config change to payment-service, a failing downstream dependency (e.g. payment provider or database), and a checkout-side change triggering bad requests to payment-service.
candidate_explanations: A deployment or config change to payment-service shortly before 11:00 UTC introduced a regression causing errors.
A downstream dependency of payment-service (payment provider, database, or internal service) degraded around 11:00 UTC and payment-service errors are propagating.
A change in checkout-service (deployment, flag, or payload change) is sending invalid or unusual requests that payment-service rejects.
An infrastructure event (capacity, network, or certificate/credential expiry) affecting payment-service or its dependencies.

tasks.objective: Characterise the error signatures in payment-service and checkout-service logs and metrics from 10:00 to 11:30 UTC: which error types and status codes dominate, the exact onset time of the rise above baseline, whether errors are concentrated on specific endpoints, pods, regions or payment methods, and whether checkout errors are upstream calls to payment-service.

List all deployments, config changes, feature flag changes and infra events for payment-service, checkout-service and their direct dependencies in the 2 hours before 11:00 UTC on 2026-09-08, with timestamps, and identify any change that occurred close to the error onset.

Map the dependency graph of payment-service and checkout-service and check health of each direct downstream dependency (payment provider integrations, databases, internal services) during 10:00 to 11:30 UTC; also check past incident postmortems for similar payment-service error patterns and their causes.

Characterise the error signatures in payment-service and checkout-service logs and metrics from 10:00 to 11:30 UTC: which error types and status codes dominate, the exact onset time of the rise above baseline, whether errors are concentrated on specific endpoints, pods, regions or payment methods, and whether checkout errors are upstream calls to payment-service.

findings.summary: payment-service error rate jumped from a ~0.2% baseline to ~21% at 11:00:00Z and peaked at 23.55% at 11:10. checkout-service error rate jumped from ~0.3% to ~9.6% at the same 11:00:00 bucket. Checkout's WARN logs in the window are almost entirely 'payment-service returned 500 Internal Server Error', so checkout's failures look like upstream calls to payment-service failing. payment-service's own logs could not be retrieved (timeouts), so endpoint, pod, region and payment-method breakdowns are not established.

observations.statement: checkout-service error_rate was 0.25–0.35% from 10:00 to 10:55, then 9.61% at 11:00:00, 8.37% at 11:05, 9.33% at 11:10, and 9.35% at 11:30.
payment-service latency_p99_ms stayed within 434–465 ms across the window, with no step change at 11:00 (464.94 at 11:00, 434.6 at 11:30).
payment-service cpu_pct (31.7–33.8%), memory_pct (53–57%) and request_rate (57.8–62.3 req/s) show no step change at 11:00.
checkout-service cpu_pct, memory_pct, latency_p99_ms (308–332 ms) and request_rate showed no step change at 11:00.

Checkout WARN/ERROR logs from 10:00 to 11:30 total 27 lines: 26 WARN and 1 ERROR. 25 are 'payment-service returned 500 Internal Server Error for order #'. The first is at 11:00:14Z, and they continue to 11:30:00Z at roughly 1–2 minute spacing. One is 'retrying idempotent call to payment-service (attempt 2)' at 10:29:28Z, before the onset. One is 'order rejected: card declined by issuer' at 11:05:54Z.
The one checkout ERROR line is a card-decline from the issuer, not a 500. Its count is a single line, so it does not characterise the bulk of the failures.

Log queries for payment-service failed on every attempt: a full-window WARN query, an ERROR-only 10:55–11:05 query, and a 11:00–11:01 query all timed out after 3 attempts each. No payment-service log lines were returned.
Checkout's 500 log lines carry no status-code detail beyond '500', no endpoint, and no pod, region or payment-method fields.

interpretations.statement: Checkout's elevated error rate starts in the same minute as payment-service's error-rate step (11:00), and checkout's logged failures are 500s from payment-service calls. This is consistent with checkout errors being a downstream effect of payment-service 500s.

The 500 errors are dominated by a server-side error from payment-service, not by issuer declines. Only one decline appears in checkout logs, and payment-service's error rate (~21–23%) is far higher than checkout's (~9%), which is consistent with checkout retries or partial-order paths absorbing some failures.

Resource saturation in payment-service and checkout-service (CPU, memory, latency, request rate) does not appear to be the trigger, since none of those signals changed at 11:00. A cause such as a deploy, dependency or config change is more plausible, but that is not checked here.

Checkout's error-rate rise is roughly 40% of payment-service's (9.5% vs 21%). That suggests checkout failures are only part of the payment failures, or that checkout's retry logic softens the error rate. Whether checkout errors are only upstream payment-service calls is supported by the logs, but the payment-service side is not confirmed.

data_gaps: payment-service logs could not be retrieved: three queries (full window WARN, 10:55–11:05 ERROR, and 11:00–11:01) each timed out after 3 attempts. Error signatures, status-code distribution, and the endpoint, pod, region and payment-method breakdowns for payment-service are therefore unknown.
Whether payment-service's 500s are the same errors that checkout reports, or whether there are additional payment-service error types, cannot be confirmed from its own logs.
The status-code mix (500 vs other codes) is inferred only from checkout's quoted messages; no payment-service status-code data was obtained.
Endpoint, pod, region and payment-method concentration could not be checked for either service. The checkout log lines do not carry those dimensions.
No change-history, deploy or dependency-health data was queried, so the trigger for the 11:00 onset is not established.
The 10:00–10:59 baseline for logs is also missing on payment-service, so the baseline error signature is unknown.
suggested_followups: Retry payment-service log queries later or with a different backend path to get its ERROR/WARN signatures, status codes and endpoint/pod/region/payment-method fields around 11:00.
Check payment-service and checkout-service deploy and config change history for ~10:45–11:00Z.
Check payment-service's downstream dependencies (for example the card-processing or issuer integration) for failures starting at 11:00Z.
Break down the payment-service error_rate metric by endpoint, pod, region or payment method if those series are available.
Confirm whether checkout's retry logic is masking part of the payment-service failures.

critique.summary: The leading hypothesis H1 (v3.2.0 deploy at 10:57Z causing payment write failures) is plausible and the timing fits, but its support is largely circumstantial. No payment-service log line was ever retrieved, so the write-path error signature is unobserved, and the schema migration status is unknown. The analysis also cites contradicting evidence (M32, M34, M35, M36, M37-M41) as contradictions but those are flat-signal observations that do not discriminate between deploy and external-provider causes. Confidence 0.55 for H1 is somewhat high given no error-type evidence; no further investigation is possible, so the report should be revised to reflect uncertainty and to state H1 as the leading candidate pending confirmation rather than as established.

issues.detail: Confidence 0.55 rests on timing alone plus a write-path mechanism that was never observed in payment-service logs, which all timed out. The reasoning admits the signature is inferred, yet confidence is not reduced accordingly. Confidence should be lower and labelled as unverified.

The claim that the deploy is the trigger rests on the onset coinciding with C09 three minutes earlier, which the critique notes is the trap of blaming a change only because it happened near onset. Nothing in the ledger ties the deploy to the failing path (no error logs, no endpoint split, no migration record). A competing cause that also starts near 11:00 with flat local signals (an external provider rejection, which the analysis itself says is not excluded) fits the evidence equally well and is not ruled out.

payment-provider is an external dependency with no metrics, no logs, and only a shallow status-page check. The sharp step at 11:00 with flat local latency, CPU and request rate is equally consistent with a discrete provider-side rejection. Labelling it as weakly supported at 0.15 because of a status page that the analysis calls shallow is inconsistent with that caveat. Telemetry absence is not evidence against it.

Checkout's 9.5% error rate is about 40% of payment-service's 21%, yet the analysis treats checkout errors as downstream propagation of payment-service 500s. Checkout's 500 messages cite only '500' with no status detail, and the 500s are not confirmed to originate from the write path. Checkout's WARN lines also do not show the endpoint, so write-path concentration is not supported.

The stated conclusion lacks payment-service error signatures entirely. This evidence cannot be obtained with the remaining budget, so the report should say the root cause is not established rather than presenting H1 as the leading conclusion.
